title: Iron Deficiency Anemia: Find the Blood Loss
bottomLine: Iron deficiency is a diagnosis and a clue. Replace iron, but also identify why iron was lost or not absorbed—especially occult GI bleeding in adults and heavy menstrual bleeding in reproductive-age patients.
recognize: Microcytosis, low ferritin, fatigue, pica and restless legs can occur, but early iron deficiency may be normocytic.
differentiate: Thalassemia trait can cause microcytosis with relatively preserved RBC count and normal iron stores; inflammation can raise ferritin despite iron restriction.
assessment: Assess diet, heavy menses, pregnancy, GI symptoms/bleeding, blood donation, NSAID use, celiac risk and prior bariatric surgery.
workup: Use CBC and ferritin with inflammatory context; investigate GI or gynecologic blood loss based on age/sex/risk rather than simply prescribing iron indefinitely.
management: Use oral iron when effective/tolerated and IV iron when oral therapy is ineffective, poorly absorbed or too slow for the clinical need.
medicationSafety: Iron causes GI side effects and can be toxic to children; counsel on safe storage.
redFlags: Unexplained iron deficiency in an older adult
counselling: Explain administration strategies and that stool darkening is common.
followUp: Document hemoglobin response and repletion of stores, then close the loop on the cause.
examTrap: Treating iron deficiency in an older adult without evaluating occult blood loss.
oneLinePearl: Iron deficiency asks two questions: how do we replace it, and where did it go?

oneLinePearl.title: Macrocytosis: B12, Folate, Alcohol, Marrow, or Medication?
oneLinePearl.bottomLine: Macrocytosis is not synonymous with B12 deficiency. Check neurologic features, diet/malabsorption, alcohol, liver/thyroid disease, medications and marrow disease; treat B12 deficiency promptly when neurologic injury is possible.
recognize: B12 deficiency can cause paresthesias, gait change and cognitive symptoms even before severe anemia.
differentiate: Folate deficiency causes megaloblastic anemia but not the classic B12 neurologic syndrome; reticulocytosis can also raise MCV.
assessment: Assess vegan/restrictive diet, pernicious anemia, GI surgery, metformin/PPI exposure, alcohol and neurologic symptoms.
workup: CBC/smear, B12 and targeted folate/TSH/liver/reticulocyte studies; methylmalonic acid can clarify borderline B12 results.
management: Replace B12 by oral or parenteral route according to cause/severity; address folate after B12 deficiency is considered.
medicationSafety: Folate alone can correct anemia while allowing B12 neurologic damage to progress.
counselling: Explain lifelong replacement when irreversible malabsorption/pernicious anemia is present.
followUp: Recheck hematologic response and neurologic recovery.
oneLinePearl.examTrap: Giving folate alone for macrocytosis before considering B12 deficiency.
oneLinePearl.oneLinePearl: Never let folate hide a B12 neurologic problem.

oneLinePearl.title: Hemolysis: Is the Marrow Keeping Up?
oneLinePearl.bottomLine: Hemolysis is suggested by anemia with reticulocytosis, indirect hyperbilirubinemia, elevated LDH and low haptoglobin. The urgent question is whether hemolysis is immune, mechanical, infectious, inherited or microangiopathic.
recognize: Jaundice, dark urine, splenomegaly and fatigue may occur.
differentiate: TMA/TTP adds thrombocytopenia and organ injury; autoimmune hemolysis can have a positive direct antiglobulin test.
assessment: Ask transfusion, medications, infection, autoimmune disease, prosthetic valves, pregnancy and family/ethnic history.
workup: Use CBC/smear, reticulocytes, bilirubin, LDH, haptoglobin and DAT; schistocytes plus thrombocytopenia requires urgent TMA assessment.
management: Stabilize severe anemia and treat cause; suspected TTP is a hematologic emergency requiring immediate specialist plasma-exchange pathway.
medicationSafety: Do not wait for the full pentad of TTP before escalating suspected microangiopathic hemolysis.
counselling: Explain triggers and recurrence risk for inherited or immune conditions.
followUp: Track hemoglobin and hemolysis markers through cause-specific care.
oneLinePearl.examTrap: Diagnosing iron deficiency from anemia alone when the smear and bilirubin indicate hemolysis.
oneLinePearl.oneLinePearl: Anemia plus high reticulocytes asks where the red cells are being lost or destroyed.

oneLinePearl.title: Thrombocytopenia: Bleeding Risk and Mechanism
oneLinePearl.bottomLine: First confirm the platelet count is real, then decide whether thrombocytopenia reflects decreased production, destruction/consumption, sequestration or dilution. Bleeding, neurologic/renal injury, pregnancy or heparin exposure raises urgency.
recognize: Petechiae and mucosal bleeding are typical of platelet disorders; spontaneous major bleeding risk rises as counts become very low but context matters.
differentiate: Pseudothrombocytopenia from platelet clumping should be excluded in a stable asymptomatic patient.
TTP, DIC, HIT and HELLP are time-critical causes.
assessment: Review infection, medications/heparin, alcohol/liver disease, pregnancy, autoimmune disease and bleeding.
workup: Repeat count/smear, coagulation and hemolysis studies according to phenotype; use HIT probability scoring before ordering HIT tests.
management: Treat cause; urgent hematology for TTP/severe ITP or unexplained profound thrombocytopenia; stop heparin and use non-heparin anticoagulation when HIT is sufficiently likely.
medicationSafety: Platelet transfusion is not routine for TTP and can be harmful unless life-threatening bleeding/procedure requires it.
counselling: Avoid NSAIDs/contact trauma when bleeding risk is clinically significant.
followUp: Trend platelets and ensure the diagnostic cause is resolved.
oneLinePearl.examTrap: Ordering HIT antibody testing for every low platelet count without estimating clinical probability.
oneLinePearl.oneLinePearl: Confirm the count, then classify production versus destruction/consumption.

oneLinePearl.title: Febrile Neutropenia: Antibiotics Are Time-Critical
oneLinePearl.bottomLine: Fever with significant neutropenia after chemotherapy or marrow disease is an oncologic emergency. Obtain cultures promptly but start appropriate broad antipseudomonal antibiotics without avoidable delay.
recognize: Inflammatory signs can be muted; sepsis may present with only fever, malaise or hypotension.
differentiate: Neutropenic fever may have no obvious source; absence of pus or leukocytosis does not reassure.
assessment: Assess hemodynamics, line sites, mouth, lungs, abdomen/perianal symptoms, urinary symptoms and recent chemotherapy.
workup: CBC/differential, blood cultures from appropriate sites and targeted imaging/labs; avoid rectal temperatures/exams when mucosal injury risk is high.
management: Use immediate empiric antipseudomonal antibiotics and risk-based admission/outpatient oncology pathways; unstable patients need sepsis resuscitation.
medicationSafety: Do not delay antibiotics waiting for ANC confirmation when a known high-risk chemotherapy patient is septic.
counselling: Teach patients on myelosuppressive therapy exactly when fever requires emergency contact.
followUp: Coordinate culture results and oncology-directed duration/G-CSF decisions.
oneLinePearl.examTrap: Giving acetaminophen and observing a febrile chemotherapy patient at home while waiting for morning blood work.
oneLinePearl.oneLinePearl: Fever plus neutropenia is antibiotics now, source later.
sourceBasis: Cancer Care Ontario/Canadian oncology febrile neutropenia practice resources

oneLinePearl.title: Lymphadenopathy: Reactive Node or Malignancy Signal?
oneLinePearl.bottomLine: Most acute tender nodes are reactive, but persistent, hard/fixed, supraclavicular or generalized nodes with constitutional symptoms require a malignancy/systemic-disease workup.
recognize: Recent URI, dental/skin infection and EBV commonly cause reactive adenopathy.
differentiate: Lymphoma often causes persistent painless adenopathy; metastatic nodes depend on drainage territory.
assessment: Assess duration, location, size, tenderness, fixation, generalized versus local distribution, fever/night sweats/weight loss, infection/exposure and medications.
workup: Use CBC and targeted infectious testing; ultrasound can characterize superficial nodes, but persistent suspicious nodes often need tissue diagnosis rather than repeated imaging alone.
management: Treat clear infection, observe low-risk reactive nodes with planned reassessment, and refer suspicious persistent adenopathy for biopsy pathway.
medicationSafety: Avoid empiric corticosteroids before tissue diagnosis when lymphoma is plausible because they can obscure pathology.
counselling: Provide a defined reassessment interval rather than 'watch it' without a plan.
followUp: Document node resolution or proceed to tissue diagnosis.
oneLinePearl.examTrap: Giving steroids for unexplained persistent lymphadenopathy before biopsy.
oneLinePearl.oneLinePearl: Suspicious lymph nodes need tissue, not repeated steroid trials.

oneLinePearl.title: Monoclonal Protein: MGUS or Multiple Myeloma?
oneLinePearl.bottomLine: An incidental monoclonal protein is not automatically myeloma, but anemia, renal dysfunction, hypercalcemia, bone pain/lytic lesions or other myeloma-defining features require urgent hematology assessment.
recognize: Myeloma can present with fractures, back pain, recurrent infections, anemia or kidney injury.
differentiate: MGUS lacks myeloma-defining organ damage and has lower clonal burden, but requires risk-based follow-up.
assessment: Ask bone pain, fractures, infection, neuropathy, weight loss and renal symptoms.
workup: Use CBC, calcium, creatinine, serum/urine monoclonal protein studies and free light chains, with imaging/marrow evaluation under hematology when indicated.
management: Refer suspected myeloma promptly; MGUS follow-up depends on risk category.
medicationSafety: NSAIDs and dehydration can worsen kidney injury in plasma-cell disease.
counselling: Explain that MGUS is not cancer but is monitored because a minority progresses.
oneLinePearl.examTrap: Reassuring an older adult with monoclonal protein and new anemia/renal dysfunction that it is just MGUS.
oneLinePearl.oneLinePearl: Monoclonal protein plus organ damage is not benign until proven otherwise.

oneLinePearl.title: Oncologic Emergencies: The Cancer Diagnosis Does Not Explain Everything
oneLinePearl.bottomLine: Cancer patients with acute deterioration require rapid recognition of spinal cord compression, superior vena cava syndrome, tumor lysis, hypercalcemia, neutropenic sepsis and other treatment complications. New symptoms should not be dismissed as expected cancer burden.
recognize: Back pain/weakness suggests cord compression; facial/upper-extremity swelling suggests SVC obstruction; electrolyte derangement after therapy can signal tumor lysis.
differentiate: Opioid effects, PE, infection and metabolic causes commonly coexist with cancer.
assessment: Assess ABCs, neurologic deficits, treatment timing, tumor type, fever, volume status and current antineoplastic drugs.
workup: Use syndrome-specific urgent MRI/CT, CBC, electrolytes, uric acid, calcium, renal function and cultures.
management: Stabilize and activate oncology/critical-care pathways; treat cord compression, sepsis, TLS and severe hypercalcemia immediately.
medicationSafety: Cancer therapies have specific cardiotoxic, immunologic, thrombotic and infection risks; medication reconciliation must include oral and infused agents.
counselling: Give treatment-specific emergency symptoms before patients leave oncology care.
followUp: Ensure handoff between acute care and oncology includes therapy held/restarted and pending results.
oneLinePearl.examTrap: Assuming severe new back pain in a cancer patient is ordinary musculoskeletal pain without a neurologic exam.
oneLinePearl.oneLinePearl: Cancer changes the emergency differential; it does not eliminate it.
sourceBasis: Cancer Care Ontario oncologic emergency resources

oneLinePearl.title: Anticoagulant Bleeding: Severity, Drug, Timing, Reversal
oneLinePearl.bottomLine: Major bleeding on anticoagulation requires rapid stabilization, identification of the anticoagulant and last dose, renal function, bleeding site and cause-specific reversal. Minor bleeding does not justify automatic permanent discontinuation.
recognize: Critical-site bleeding, hemodynamic compromise, significant hemoglobin drop or transfusion need defines major bleeding clinically.
differentiate: DOAC effect is not reliably measured by INR; warfarin reversal differs from factor-Xa or dabigatran reversal.
assessment: Assess ABCs, bleeding source, last dose, renal function, interacting drugs, antiplatelets and anticoagulation indication.
workup: CBC, coagulation tests appropriate to drug, renal function, type/cross and source-directed imaging/endoscopy.
management: Hold anticoagulant, control source and use specific or nonspecific reversal according to agent/severity; restart decisions require balancing thrombosis and rebleeding.
medicationSafety: Vitamin K reverses warfarin but not DOACs; PCC and specific antidotes have agent-specific roles.
counselling: After stabilization, review NSAIDs, alcohol, duplicate antiplatelets and adherence.
followUp: Document when/why anticoagulation is restarted or permanently stopped.
oneLinePearl.examTrap: Using INR to decide whether apixaban has clinically important anticoagulant effect.
oneLinePearl.oneLinePearl: Bleeding reversal starts by naming the anticoagulant and the last dose.
sourceBasis: Thrombosis Canada DOAC bleeding and warfarin clinical guides

oneLinePearl.title: Cancer-Associated VTE: Clot and Bleeding Risks Both Matter
oneLinePearl.bottomLine: Active cancer increases recurrent VTE risk, so anticoagulation is generally continued while cancer remains active if bleeding risk is acceptable. Agent choice depends on cancer site, thrombocytopenia, GI/GU bleeding risk, interactions and patient preference.
recognize: Cancer-associated thrombosis may be symptomatic or incidental on staging imaging.
differentiate: GI/GU cancers and thrombocytopenia can favour LMWH over a DOAC in selected patients.
assessment: Assess clot burden, bleeding history, platelet count, renal function, cancer site/stage, chemotherapy interactions and goals of care.
workup: Use standard VTE imaging and baseline blood counts/renal function.
management: Use LMWH or anti-Xa DOACs according to current Thrombosis Canada guidance and individual bleeding risk; reassess duration while cancer activity/risk evolves.
medicationSafety: Drug interactions with anticancer therapy and thrombocytopenia can alter anticoagulant choice/dose.
counselling: Discuss injection burden, cost and bleeding signs as part of shared choice.
followUp: Reassess every few months while cancer remains active and again near end of life.
oneLinePearl.examTrap: Choosing a DOAC automatically for every cancer-associated clot without considering GI cancer bleeding risk.
oneLinePearl.oneLinePearl: Cancer VTE therapy is anticoagulation plus a bleeding-risk and interaction check.
sourceBasis: Thrombosis Canada Cancer and Thrombosis clinical guide

oneLinePearl.title: VTE Duration: Provoked, Persistent, Recurrent, or Preference-Sensitive?
oneLinePearl.bottomLine: Anticoagulation duration after VTE depends on provoking factors, persistent risk, recurrence, bleeding risk and patient preferences. A major resolved transient trigger usually supports finite therapy, while active cancer or high-risk persistent thrombophilia often supports continuation.
recognize: Surgery-provoked VTE has lower recurrence risk after treatment than unprovoked or persistent-risk VTE.
differentiate: Not all 'unprovoked' VTE requires lifelong full-dose anticoagulation; current Canadian guidance emphasizes individualized extended-therapy decisions.
assessment: Classify provoking factor strength, prior VTE, cancer, thrombophilia, bleeding risk, renal function and patient preference.
workup: Do not order indiscriminate thrombophilia panels if results will not change management.
management: Treat acute VTE for the required initial period, then use current Thrombosis Canada recurrence/bleeding framework; reduced-dose DOAC is preferred for many patients continuing extended secondary prevention.
medicationSafety: Reassess bleeding risk at least annually when long-term anticoagulation continues.
counselling: Discuss absolute clot-versus-bleeding tradeoffs rather than presenting indefinite therapy as automatic.
followUp: Revisit the decision as comorbidity and preference change.
oneLinePearl.examTrap: Ordering a thrombophilia panel after a clearly surgery-provoked first DVT with no plan to change treatment based on results.
oneLinePearl.oneLinePearl: Duration is a recurrence-versus-bleeding decision, not a fixed rule for every clot.
sourceBasis: Thrombosis Canada VTE Duration of Treatment clinical guide 2026

oneLinePearl.title: Cancer Survivorship: Recurrence, Late Effects, and Primary Care
oneLinePearl.bottomLine: Cancer survivors need ordinary preventive care plus treatment-specific surveillance and late-effect monitoring. More imaging is not automatically better; follow the disease-specific survivorship plan and manage cardiovascular, bone, endocrine, fertility and psychosocial sequelae.
recognize: Late effects depend on prior chemotherapy, immunotherapy, radiation and surgery.
differentiate: New symptoms can represent recurrence, a late effect or an unrelated common disease; avoid diagnostic anchoring.
assessment: Maintain a treatment summary, recurrence symptoms, secondary-cancer risk, cardiovascular/metabolic health, bone health, fertility/sexual function and mental health.
workup: Order surveillance only at guideline-supported intervals and investigate new symptoms diagnostically.
management: Coordinate oncology and primary care, vaccinations, rehabilitation, lymphedema and chronic disease prevention.
medicationSafety: Check prior cardiotoxic or immunologic therapies before attributing new symptoms to ordinary disease.
counselling: Give a clear survivorship care plan and identify who owns each surveillance task.
followUp: Use risk-based long-term follow-up rather than generic annual scans.
oneLinePearl.examTrap: Ordering whole-body imaging routinely for an asymptomatic survivor without a guideline indication.
oneLinePearl.oneLinePearl: Survivorship care is targeted surveillance plus excellent primary care.
